title: Insert a Node at the Head of a Linked List
directAnswer: Make a new node, point its next at the current head, and return the new node as the new head. Two lines, no traversal — O(1) time, O(1) space. The only thing you must not forget is returning the new head, because the head pointer changes.

remember.pattern: Prepend: new node's next = old head, return new node
remember.formula:
newNode = ListNode(data)
newNode.next = head
return newNode
rules: Set `newNode.next = head` **before** returning — this links the new node to the rest of the list.
**Return the new head.** Prepending always changes the head, so the caller must receive `newNode`.
No walk is needed — head insertion is O(1); never loop to the end.
An empty list (`head == null`) is not special: `newNode.next = null` makes the new node the sole element.
Don't mutate the old head's pointers — only the new node's `next` is set.
whenToUse: Push onto the front of a singly linked list (stack-like LIFO behaviour)
Build a list in reverse order of arrival in O(1) per insert
Prepend without knowing or caring about the list length
Implementing a stack or an adjacency list on top of linked nodes
antiSignals: You must insert at a specific middle index → walk to position − 1 first (insert at position)
You must append to the back and order matters → keep a tail pointer for O(1), else it's O(n)
You need a queue (FIFO) → head-insert alone gives a stack; pair with tail tracking for a queue
remember.takeaway: Head insertion is the cheapest list edit: point the new node at the old head and return it. It's O(1), it's how a linked-list stack pushes, and it's the position-0 case that every insert-at-position solution special-cases.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you understand that prepending is O(1) (no traversal) and that the head pointer changes, so the function must return the new head.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting to return the new node (so the caller keeps the old head), or setting head = newNode locally without linking newNode.next to the old head.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State that it's O(1), that the head changes so you return the new node, and that this is exactly a stack push and the position-0 branch of insert-at-position.

problemStatement:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list and an integer `data`.

Create a **new node** holding `data` and insert it at the **front** of the list, so it becomes the new head. Return *the head of the modified list*.
constraints: The list is singly linked (next pointers only)
Insertion must run in O(1) time
understanding: Prepending means the new node sits before every existing node. Since nothing after it changes, we only set the new node's next to the old head and report the new node as the head — no scanning, no other pointer edits.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should the new node become the head, or go after the head?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Become the head — it sits in front of the current first node, which is what 'insert at head' means.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What happens if the list is empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The new node becomes the only node: its next is null and it's returned as the head. No special branch needed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I allocate a new node or reuse one?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Allocate a new node holding data — we're inserting a fresh element, not moving an existing one.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the function need to return anything?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the new head. Prepending always changes the head, so the caller relies on the return value.

examples.explanation: New node 1 points at the old head 2 and becomes the head.
Empty list: newNode.next = null; the new node is the sole element and the head.
New node 7 points at 9 and becomes the head.

diagrams.title: The whole operation in two links
diagrams.caption: Prepending is constant time: link the new node to the old head and return it — no traversal.

approaches.name: Prepend — Link New Node to Old Head (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: This is the whole answer. Say it's O(1) and that the head changes, so you return the new node.
hints: The new node must come before everything that exists now. What single pointer makes that true?
If the new node's next points at the current head, the new node is now first. What do you hand back to the caller?
Do you need to look at any other node, or even know the list's length, to prepend?
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two pointer assignments and a return, independent of list size → O(1) time. One new node, no extra structures → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
We create the node and splice it in front of the list with a single link.

**Why no traversal.** Prepending touches only the front. The new node needs to point at whatever is currently first (the head), and nothing downstream changes — so there's nothing to walk. That's what makes it O(1), in contrast to appending (which is O(n) without a tail pointer).

**Link before returning.** Set `newNode.next = head` so the new node connects to the existing chain. If you skip this, the new node points at null and you've dropped the entire old list. The order is: build node, link its next to the old head, return the node.

**Why we return the new head.** The head pointer moves to the new node. A function that edits the list in place can't change the caller's head variable in languages that pass references by value, so the convention is to return the (possibly new) head and let the caller reassign. Head insertion *always* changes the head, making the return essential here.

**Why empty lists need no branch.** If `head` is null, `newNode.next = null` is exactly right — the new node becomes a one-element list. The same two lines cover empty and non-empty inputs.
approaches.insight: Head insertion is the position-0 special case of insert-at-position, lifted out on its own: no predecessor to find, so no walk — just link and return. It's also precisely how a stack built on a linked list pushes.

dryRun.intro: Build node 1, point it at the old head 2, return it as the new head.

java.explanation: Allocate the node that will become the new head.
Link it to the current head so the rest of the list follows.
The head changed — return the new node so the caller can reassign.

python.explanation: Point it at the old head; this works even when head is None.
Return the new head — prepending always changes it.

diagrams.title: New node becomes the front
diagrams.caption: Top row is the chain. The new node 1 links to the old head and takes its place at the front.

pitfalls: Not returning the new node — the caller keeps the old head and never sees the inserted element.
Forgetting newNode.next = head — the new node points at null and the rest of the list is lost.
Walking the list before inserting — needless O(n) work; prepending is O(1).
Mutating the old head's pointers — unnecessary and can corrupt the list.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to return the new node, so the head change never reaches the caller.
Not linking newNode.next to the old head, dropping the existing list.
Traversing to the tail before inserting — that's append, not prepend.
Assuming the empty list needs a special branch when it doesn't.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Setting head locally without returning it
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Reassigning a local parameter doesn't change the caller's variable in languages that pass references by value. The new node is built and linked but never reaches the caller, who still holds the old head.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Skipping the link to the old head
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Returning the new node without pointing its next at the old head leaves newNode.next as null, so the rest of the list is detached and lost.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
new_node = ListNode(data)
return new_node   # new_node.next is None — old list dropped
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
new_node = ListNode(data)
new_node.next = head
return new_node

patternNote: Constant-time prepend: link the new node to the old head and return it. It's the position-0 case of insert-at-position and the push operation of a linked-list stack.
